What moves the price on a B4204T37 replacement is whether the PCV system, timing belt, tensioner and water pump have been addressed on the donor unit. failures.title: Volvo B4204T37 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: PCV System Clogging - all VEA T5 variants including B4204T37
items.whatHappens: Crankcase ventilation (PCV) system becomes clogged with sludge and carbon deposits, increasing crankcase pressure and forcing oil past piston rings and turbo seals. Symptoms include increased oil consumption (some owners report 1 litre per 1,000 km), blue smoke from the exhaust, and possible oil leaks from seals. If left unchecked, it can lead to turbo damage and accelerated engine wear.
items.repairVsReplace: PCV system cleaning or replacement (typically £300-£600) resolves the issue if caught early. If oil consumption has been ignored, the turbocharger may be damaged and require replacement (£800-£1,500). In advanced cases with piston ring gumming, a full rebuild or replacement is the only definitive fix. Read our full oil consumption guide

items.title: Timing Belt - interference engine, critical interval
items.whatHappens: The B4204T37 uses a timing belt, not a chain. As an interference engine, a failed belt or tensioner causes pistons to strike valves, destroying the cylinder head and often the bottom end. The interval is typically 90,000 miles or 10 years, but many specialists recommend earlier replacement (80,000 miles) due to reports of belt and tensioner wear on VEA petrol engines.
items.repairVsReplace: Belt failure is catastrophic - full engine replacement is almost always required. Preventative belt replacement at the correct interval is essential; many specialists recommend replacing the water pump, tensioner and VVT pulleys simultaneously. Read our full timing belt failure guide

items.title: VVT Cam Timing Sensor / Solenoid Issues
items.whatHappens: The VVT (variable valve timing) solenoids can become clogged or fail, causing rough idle, loss of power, or engine management lights (P0010, P0011, etc.). This is less common on the B4204T37 than on earlier Ford‑derived units, but still a known issue on higher‑mileage VEA engines.
items.repairVsReplace: VVT solenoid replacement (£200-£400 each) is straightforward. If the issue is caused by oil sludge, a full oil change and engine flush may be needed.

failures.goodYearsLine: The B4204T37 is a later VEA variant (2016+) with improved PCV design and revised belt tensioners compared to early VEA units (2013-2015). However, the timing belt remains a critical service item, and PCV systems still require attention on higher‑mileage cars. Regular oil changes with the correct 0W‑20 VCC RBS0‑2AE spec are essential to prevent sludge‑related issues.

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the B4204T37
variants.intro: The B4204T37 is a specific sub‑code within the VEA 2.0‑litre T5 family, introduced around 2016 as an updated calibration. It sits between the earlier B4204T11 (2014‑2016) and the later B4204T23 (2017‑2020) in the VEA timeline. Here's how it compares to other common VEA T5 codes: - B4204T11 - 245hp, 2014‑2016, earlier VEA T5, slightly lower output - B4204T20 - 249hp AWD, 2015‑2018, similar to T37 but with AWD‑specific calibration - B4204T37 - approx. 245‑254hp, 2016‑present, the standard FWD T5 tune for many models after 2016 - B4204T23 - 254hp, 2017‑2020, later calibration with revised emission controls - B4204T27 - 320hp T6 twin‑charged (supercharger + turbo) - completely different configuration Where the code is found: The B4204T37 sub‑code is printed on a sticker on the timing belt cover and on the V5C registration document under "Engine number". The first three characters (B42) indicate the engine family, and the final digits give the specific variant. Commonly confused codes: The B4204T37 is often mistaken for the B4204T11 or B4204T20, but they are not identical - they have different ECU calibrations and sometimes different injector part numbers. Fitting the wrong variant can result in incorrect fuelling and limp mode. Always match the exact sub‑code when buying a replacement.

relatives.description: B4204T11 (2.0L T5, 2014-2016): The earlier VEA 2.0‑litre T5 calibration that preceded the B4204T37. The T11 produced 245hp and was fitted from 2014-2016; the B4204T37 was the updated calibration with improved emissions and drivability. Both are VEA architecture, but the T37 has revised software and injector part numbers - not a straight swap without matching ECU and injectors.

B4204T23 (2.0L T5, 2017-2020): The later VEA T5 calibration that followed the B4204T37, producing 254hp with further emissions refinements. The T23 is the most powerful single‑turbo T5 and is considered the most refined of the VEA petrols. If you're replacing a B4204T37, the T23 is a potential upgrade but requires ECU matching and potentially different injectors.

B4204T27 (2.0L T6, 320hp twin‑charged): The high‑performance T6 variant of the VEA family - supercharged and turbocharged, producing 320hp. Shares the same block but has a supercharger, different ancillaries, and a completely different induction system. Not interchangeable with the T5; if you're looking for T6, you're on the wrong page.

D4204T (2.0L D4 diesel): The diesel counterpart in the VEA family - shares the same block architecture but is fundamentally different in fuelling, compression, turbo and ancillaries. If your car is diesel, you're on the wrong page.

B4204T44 / T46 (T5 PHEV hybrid variants): The hybrid versions of the VEA T5 - petrol engine combined with an electric motor. They share the block but include additional hybrid components and a different starter‑generator; not a direct swap with non‑hybrid T5 units.

relatives.code: The B4204T37 is a Volvo‑only VEA engine, not shared with any other manufacturer. It is not related to the Ford 2.0 EcoBoost, despite both being 2.0‑litre turbos; the VEA architecture is Volvo's own design and shares no parts with Ford.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement B4204T37 - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: ** A used B4204T37 can make sense for older S60, V60 or XC60 examples where the car's value is under £5,000. **Crucially:** only buy a used unit with documented PCV service history, timing belt replacement record, and proof of regular oil changes with the correct 0W‑20 VCC spec. A used engine without these risks inheriting the same PCV and timing issues - which could cost you the equivalent of a reconditioned unit in repairs. Used engines service

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: ** A proper B4204T37 recon addresses the PCV system, timing belt, tensioner, water pump, VVT pulleys, injector seals and a full oil system flush - exactly the maintenance items that keep these engines running well into high mileage. This is the right call for any car worth over £6,000 where you plan to keep it for 2+ years. Most recon units come with a 12‑month warranty and have had all the common issues proactively fixed. Reconditioned engines service

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: ** A full B4204T37 rebuild is rarely cost‑effective compared to a reconditioned exchange unit - the labour to strip, inspect and rebuild a VEA petrol with new pistons, rings, bearings and cylinder head overhaul typically exceeds £4,000 before parts. Only consider a rebuild for a low‑mileage, high‑spec car (e.g. an XC90 T5 Inscription or a V90 T5) where the chassis is immaculate and you have a Volvo specialist who knows the VEA platform intimately. Rebuilt engines service

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: ** All replacement engines through our network are supplied with 12‑month warranty and can be fitted by Volvo specialists nationwide. Supply & fit service
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: ** The B4204T37 sits across a value range - from £4,000 S60 T5s to £25,000 XC90 T5s. For a sub‑£5,000 car, a reconditioned engine at £3,200-£4,500 may represent 70-100% of the car's value - evaluate scrap value before committing. For XC60, XC90, S90 and V90 owners, the car's retained value comfortably absorbs a recon engine cost. Be honest about the car's condition, mileage and MOT history before deciding.

items.answer: The most common issues are PCV system clogging (leading to increased oil consumption) and timing belt wear on an interference engine - both of which can lead to catastrophic engine damage if ignored. The B4204T37 is a later VEA variant with improved components over early units, but the PCV system still requires attention at higher mileages, and the timing belt must be replaced at the recommended interval (90,000 miles or 8-10 years). Regular oil changes with the correct 0W‑20 VCC RBS0‑2AE spec are essential to prevent sludge‑related issues. PCV clogging: oil consumption can exceed 1L per 1,000km. Timing belt interval: 90,000 miles or 8‑10 years - failure = full engine replacement. VVT solenoid issues possible at higher mileage.

items.question: Should I buy a used or reconditioned B4204T37 engine?
items.answer: It depends on your car's value and the service history of the donor engine. For an older S60 or V60 valued under £5,000, a used unit with documented PCV and timing belt history (£2,000-£3,200) may be the only financially sensible option. For XC60, XC90, S90 and V90 owners where the car is worth £8,000+, a reconditioned unit (£3,200-£5,000) with a 12‑month warranty and all known issues addressed is almost always the better investment - given the engine's sensitivity to PCV and timing maintenance. Used: lower cost, higher risk of inheriting PCV/timing issues. Reconditioned: all common failure points addressed, 12‑24 month warranty. Always insist on oil service history and belt change records.

items.question: What's the difference between B4204T11, B4204T20, B4204T37 and B4204T23?
items.answer: These are all VEA 2.0‑litre T5 petrol variants with different calibrations and production years. B4204T11 is 245hp (2014‑2016), B4204T20 is 249hp AWD (2015‑2018), B4204T37 is the updated FWD tune (2016‑present) with improved emissions, and B4204T23 is the later 254hp tune (2017‑2020). They share the same block but differ in ECU software, injectors, and sometimes turbo part numbers. They are not directly interchangeable without matching the ECU and ancillaries. B4204T11: 245hp, 2014‑2016, earlier VEA. B4204T20: 249hp AWD, 2015‑2018. B4204T37: 245‑254hp, 2016‑present, updated FWD tune. B4204T23: 254hp, 2017‑2020, latest calibration.

items.question: How long does a B4204T37 engine last?
items.answer: With proper maintenance - especially strict adherence to the timing belt interval and regular oil changes with the correct 0W‑20 VCC spec - 150,000-200,000 miles is achievable before major work is needed. The key factors are: (1) timing belt replacement at 90,000 miles or 8-10 years - failure is catastrophic; (2) PCV system cleaning or replacement around 80,000-100,000 miles to prevent oil consumption; (3) oil changes at 10,000 miles or annually with the correct spec. Many VEA T5 units exceed 200,000 miles with these items addressed proactively. Timing belt is the single most important service item. PCV issues typically emerge between 80,000-120,000 miles. Use only the recommended 0W‑20 oil specification.
